question: On which date did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 come into force across India?
explanation: Enforced on 1 July 2024 via MHA Notification S.O. 850(E).

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; 1 July 2024 is the statutory enforcement date.

learningObjective: Master BNS commencement date.

question: Under Section 1(4) of BNS 2023, the territorial waters of India extend into the sea up to:
explanation: Territorial waters extend to 12 nautical miles from baseline.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; 12 nautical miles is statutory limit.

learningObjective: Understand maritime territorial limits.

question: An offence was committed on 15 May 2024. The trial commenced on 10 August 2024. Under which statute must the offence be charged?
explanation: Article 20(1) bars retrospective application of substantive penal law; IPC 1860 governs pre-July 2024 offences.

optionBreakdown.A: BNS cannot apply retrospectively under Art 20(1).
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; IPC governs pre-July 2024 offences.

learningObjective: Master non-retroactivity of substantive penal law.

question: Under Section 1(5) BNS / Section 4 IPC, extraterritorial jurisdiction extends to offences committed by:
options: Any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India
Foreign nationals in foreign countries against foreigners
explanation: Section 1(5) applies to any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Indian citizens committing crimes anywhere are triable in India.

learningObjective: Master extraterritorial jurisdiction.

question: A, a foreigner, commits murder on an Indian merchant ship on the high seas. Which court in India has jurisdiction to try A?
options: Any court in India where A may be found or brought
Only the Supreme Court of India
Only the International Court of Justice
explanation: Under Section 1(5)(b) BNS / S. 4(2) IPC, jurisdiction covers any person on an Indian registered ship.

optionBreakdown.A: Indian courts have jurisdiction by registration.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; triable where found in India.
optionBreakdown.C: SC is not original trial court.
optionBreakdown.D: ICJ is for states, not criminal trials.

learningObjective: Analyze maritime jurisdiction over foreign nationals.

question: Which of the following acts cannot be punished under the general provisions of BNS 2023?
options: Offences in India by foreign citizens
Mutiny and desertion governed by Army Act, 1950
explanation: Section 1(6) BNS / Section 5 IPC preserves special military enactments.

optionBreakdown.A: Foreign citizens subject to territorial law.
optionBreakdown.B: J&K covered by BNS.
optionBreakdown.D: Territorial waters are part of India.

learningObjective: Understand savings of special penal laws.

question: In Mobarik Ali Ahmed v. State of Bombay (1957), the Supreme Court affirmed that a foreigner committing an offence in India while physically outside India is:
options: Amenable to Indian criminal jurisdiction as the offence occurred in India
Subject only to extradition without trial
explanation: Physical presence in India is not necessary if the crime took effect in India.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; corporeal presence not required.

learningObjective: Apply extraterritorial precedent.

question: Which provision of BNS replaces Section 2 of IPC concerning punishment of offences committed within India?
explanation: Section 1(3) BNS corresponds to Section 2 IPC.

optionBreakdown.B: Commencement.

learningObjective: Map BNS Section 1 sub-clauses.

question: Under Section 1(5)(c) BNS / S. 4(3) IPC, Indian courts have extraterritorial jurisdiction over any person targeting a:
explanation: Section 1(5)(c) covers cyber-attacks targeting computer resources located in India.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; computer resource located in India.

learningObjective: Understand cyber jurisdiction.

question: The phrase 'every person' in Section 1(3) BNS / Section 2 IPC includes which of the following?
options: Citizens and non-citizens, including artificial legal persons like corporations
explanation: Section 2(26) BNS / Section 11 IPC defines 'person' to include corporations and non-citizens.

optionBreakdown.B: Foreigners included.

learningObjective: Define 'person' in criminal jurisprudence.

question: The fundamental maxim 'Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea' literally translates to:
options: An act makes a man guilty only if civilly actionable
An act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty
A guilty mind alone without an act is punishable
Every illegal omission automatically constitutes actus reus
explanation: Crime requires concurrence of guilty act and guilty mind.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; act plus guilty mind required.
optionBreakdown.D: Omission must be illegal and accompanied by mens rea.

learningObjective: Master foundational criminal maxim.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four recognized stages in the commission of a crime?
explanation: Stages are Intention, Preparation, Attempt, and Commission. Motive is not a procedural stage.

optionBreakdown.B: Stage 2.
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; motive is not one of the four stages.

learningObjective: Distinguish stages of crime from motive.

question: As a general rule, preparation is not punishable. In which case is mere preparation made expressly punishable?
explanation: Section 310(2) BNS / Section 399 IPC punishes preparation to commit dacoity.

optionBreakdown.B: Not punishable.

learningObjective: Identify statutory preparation exceptions.

question: In State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George (1965), the Supreme Court held that mens rea is excluded in statutory offences when:
options: Statute expressly or by necessary implication rules out mens rea for public welfare
RBI failed to notify accused personally
explanation: Statutory exclusion of mens rea can be express or necessarily implied in socio-economic laws.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; express or implied statutory exclusion.

learningObjective: Analyze strict liability in statutory crimes.

question: Which offence under the penal code is an example of strict liability where honest belief regarding age is no defence?
explanation: In R v. Prince and Section 137 BNS / Section 361 IPC, kidnapping from lawful guardianship is strict liability regarding age.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; kidnapping is strict liability regarding age.
optionBreakdown.B: Requires intent/knowledge.

learningObjective: Recognize strict liability exceptions.

question: What is the proximity test formulated in Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar (1961) to distinguish attempt from preparation?
options: Accused does an act towards commission after completing preparation
Accused does the last possible act
explanation: Attempt commences when an act towards commission is done after completing preparation.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; active step towards execution constitutes attempt.
optionBreakdown.B: Last act doctrine rejected.

learningObjective: Distinguish attempt from preparation.

question: A puts his hand in B's pocket intending to steal money, but finds the pocket completely empty. A is guilty of:
options: Attempt to commit theft under Section 62 BNS / S. 511 IPC
explanation: Factual impossibility does not bar attempt liability; picking an empty pocket is attempt to commit theft.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; attempt to commit theft.

learningObjective: Understand attempt with factual impossibility.

question: Which mental element in criminal law signifies the highest degree of blameworthiness?
explanation: Hierarchy: Intention > Knowledge > Rashness > Negligence.

optionBreakdown.B: Reckless indifference.

learningObjective: Master degrees of mental culpability.

question: A purchases matchsticks and petrol to burn down B's house. While walking towards B's house, A is intercepted 2 km away. A has committed:
options: Attempt to commit mischief by fire
Only preparation, which is not punishable
explanation: Purchasing materials and walking is still preparation; no direct proximate step taken at the house.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; merely preparation.

learningObjective: Apply proximity test to preparation versus attempt.

question: Under Section 62 BNS / Section 511 IPC, what is the default punishment for attempt when no express provision exists?
options: One-fourth of longest term of imprisonment
One-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or fine, or both
explanation: Default penalty for attempt is up to one-half of the longest term provided for the offence.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; one-half of maximum term.

learningObjective: Recall general penalty formula for attempt.

question: How does BNS 2023 structurally organize definitions compared to IPC 1860?
options: All primary definitions consolidated alphabetically into Section 2
Abolished to leave terms to courts
explanation: Section 2 BNS consolidates definitions into clauses (1) to (39).

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; consolidated into Section 2.

learningObjective: Understand consolidation of definitions.

question: Under Section 2(10) BNS, the pronoun 'he' and its derivatives are defined to include:
options: Any person, whether male, female, or transgender
explanation: Section 2(10) BNS explicitly includes male, female, and transgender.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; includes male, female, and transgender.

learningObjective: Master gender-neutral and transgender inclusion.

question: Under Section 2(11) BNS / Section 52 IPC, nothing is said to be done in 'good faith' which is done:
explanation: Good faith requires 'due care and attention'.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; due care and attention.

learningObjective: Recall definition of good faith.

question: Who among the following is NOT a 'Public Servant' under Section 2(28) BNS 2023?
options: A commissioned officer in military forces
An arbitrator appointed by a Court
A practicing advocate in their private professional capacity
explanation: Advocates in private practice are not public servants.

optionBreakdown.A: Judges are public servants under S. 2(28)(a).
optionBreakdown.B: Officers are public servants under S. 2(28)(b).
optionBreakdown.C: Arbitrators are public servants under S. 2(28)(e).
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; private advocates are not public servants.

learningObjective: Identify who constitutes a Public Servant.

question: The definition of 'Dishonestly' under Section 2(7) BNS / Section 24 IPC requires:
options: Intention to cause injury to feelings
Intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person
Deceiving any person without financial loss
explanation: Dishonestly requires intention to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; wrongful gain or wrongful loss.

learningObjective: Define Dishonestly in criminal law.

question: In Dr. Vimla v. Delhi Administration (1963), 'fraudulently' under Section 25 IPC / Section 2(8) BNS was held to involve:
explanation: Supreme Court held fraud requires twin elements: deceit and injury.

optionBreakdown.B: Financial gain not mandatory.
optionBreakdown.C: Deceit without injury is not fraud.
optionBreakdown.D: Breach of contract is civil wrong.

learningObjective: Master elements of fraudulently.

question: Under Section 2(39) BNS / Section 44 IPC, the term 'Injury' denotes harm illegally caused to any person in:
explanation: Injury covers four dimensions: body, mind, reputation, and property.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; body, mind, reputation, property.

learningObjective: Recall four dimensions of Injury.

question: Under Section 2(26) BNS / Section 11 IPC, the word 'Person' includes:
options: Any Company or Association or body of persons, whether incorporated or not
explanation: Person includes corporations, associations, partnerships, whether incorporated or not.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; corporations and bodies of persons.

learningObjective: Define corporate and juristic persons.

question: Under Section 3(1) BNS / Section 32 IPC, an omission is punishable ONLY IF it is an:
options: Illegal omission in breach of a legal duty
Omission causing financial loss to State
explanation: Omission must be 'illegal' (an offence, prohibited by law, or furnishing ground for civil action).

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; illegal omission.

learningObjective: Distinguish legal from moral omissions.

question: Under Section 2(37) BNS / Section 52A IPC, which relationship is statutorily exempted from liability for harbouring?
options: Spouse harbouring a husband or wife
explanation: The husband or wife of the person harboured is exempted by statutory exception.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; matrimonial cohabitation exception.

learningObjective: Recognize matrimonial exemption in harbouring.

question: How many classes of punishments are recognized under Section 4 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
explanation: Section 4 BNS recognizes six punishments: Death, Imprisonment for life, Imprisonment (rigorous/simple), Forfeiture of property, Fine, and Community Service.

optionBreakdown.A: Four was under old English law.
optionBreakdown.B: Five was under Section 53 IPC.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; BNS introduces Community Service as the 6th punishment.

learningObjective: Identify the six punishments in BNS 2023.

question: Which innovative punishment was introduced for the first time in Indian general penal law under Section 4(f) BNS 2023?
explanation: Section 4(f) BNS introduces Community Service as an alternative reformative punishment for petty offences.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Community Service is newly introduced.

learningObjective: Recall the 6th punishment in BNS.

question: In which of the following offences does the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 explicitly provide Community Service as an alternative punishment?
options: First-time theft where value of stolen property is less than Rs 5,000 upon return
Robbery on highway between sunset and sunrise
Voluntarily causing grievous hurt with weapon
explanation: Under Section 303(2) Proviso BNS, theft of value less than Rs 5,000 by a first-time offender where property is returned may be punished with Community Service.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; petty theft under Rs 5,000 has community service.
optionBreakdown.B: Heinous offence with 14 years rigorous imprisonment.

learningObjective: Identify specific offences punishable with Community Service.

question: Under Section 356(2) BNS / Section 500 IPC, what new alternative punishment can the court award for Defamation?
explanation: Section 356(2) BNS provides that whoever defames another may be punished with simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Community service is added for defamation.
optionBreakdown.B: Solitary confinement max 3 months.
optionBreakdown.C: Apology not statutory penalty in code.

learningObjective: Understand community service in defamation.

question: Under Section 226 BNS (attempt to commit suicide to compel public servant), what punishment is prescribed?
options: Simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, or with community service
No punishment as suicide attempt is decriminalized
explanation: Section 226 BNS penalizes attempting suicide with intent to compel or restrain any public servant from discharging official duty with simple imprisonment up to 1 year, fine, both, or community service.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; up to 1 year, fine, or community service.
optionBreakdown.C: General suicide attempt IPC 309 is omitted, but S. 226 penalizes coercive suicide attempts.

learningObjective: Distinguish Section 226 BNS from legacy IPC Section 309.

question: Which of the following describes the meaning of 'Imprisonment for Life' in criminal law (Gopal Vinayak Godse / Maru Ram doctrine)?
options: Imprisonment for the remainder of the natural life of the convict unless commuted by Government
explanation: A sentence of imprisonment for life means imprisonment for the remaining period of the convict's natural life, subject to statutory remission/commutation.

optionBreakdown.B: 20 years is only for calculating fractions under S. 7 BNS / S. 57 IPC.

learningObjective: Define the true legal duration of Life Imprisonment.

question: Under Section 7 BNS / Section 57 IPC, in calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for:
explanation: Section 7 BNS / Section 57 IPC explicitly provides that for calculating fractions of punishment, life imprisonment is reckoned as 20 years.

optionBreakdown.A: 14 years is minimum before remission under CrPC 433A / BNSS 475.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; 20 years for fraction calculations.

learningObjective: Recall calculation of fractions for life imprisonment.

question: Under Section 355 BNS / Section 510 IPC, misconduct in public by a drunken person is punishable with simple imprisonment up to 24 hours, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or with:
explanation: Section 355 BNS adds community service as an alternative to 24-hour imprisonment or fine.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; community service.

learningObjective: Recognize community service in drunken misconduct.

question: Under Section 202 BNS / Section 168 IPC, a public servant unlawfully engaging in trade may be punished with simple imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both, or with:
explanation: Section 202 BNS introduces community service as an alternative penalty for public servants unlawfully engaging in trade.

optionBreakdown.B: Pension is service rule, not code penalty.

learningObjective: Identify community service in public servant offences.

question: Under Section 209 BNS / Section 174 IPC, non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant may be punished with simple imprisonment, fine, or with:
explanation: Section 209 BNS adds community service for non-attendance in obedience to legal summons or order.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; community service.

learningObjective: Recall community service in procedural disobedience.

question: What is the absolute maximum period of Solitary Confinement that can be awarded in any single sentence under Section 11 BNS / Section 73 IPC?
explanation: Under Section 11 BNS / Section 73 IPC, solitary confinement shall in no case exceed three (3) months in the whole.

optionBreakdown.B: Max for <= 1 year sentences.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; absolute maximum is three months.

learningObjective: Recall maximum limit of solitary confinement.

question: If the term of rigorous imprisonment awarded is 8 months, what is the maximum solitary confinement the court can order?
explanation: Scale under Section 11 BNS: term <= 6 months -> 1 month; term > 6 months and <= 1 year -> 2 months; term > 1 year -> 3 months. For 8 months, maximum is 2 months.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; up to 2 months.

learningObjective: Apply solitary confinement scale to sentences.

question: Under Section 12 BNS / Section 74 IPC, what is the maximum period of solitary confinement that can be executed at any one time?
explanation: In executing solitary confinement, it shall in no case exceed fourteen (14) days at a time, with intervals of not less than such periods.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; max 14 days at a time.

learningObjective: Recall execution limits of solitary confinement.

question: When the imprisonment awarded exceeds three months, what is the maximum solitary confinement that can be given in any ONE MONTH?
explanation: Under Section 12 BNS / Section 74 IPC, when sentence exceeds 3 months, solitary confinement shall not exceed seven (7) days in any one month, with intervals between solitary periods.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; maximum 7 days in any one month.

learningObjective: Apply monthly execution limits for long sentences.

question: Can solitary confinement be awarded to a person sentenced to Simple Imprisonment?
options: Yes, if the judge records special reasons
No, solitary confinement can ONLY be awarded where the sentence is Rigorous Imprisonment
Yes, if the convict consents in writing
explanation: Section 11 BNS / Section 73 IPC explicitly states that solitary confinement can be ordered only whenever any person is convicted of an offence for which the Court has power to sentence him to 'rigorous imprisonment'.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; strictly restricted to rigorous imprisonment.

learningObjective: Master precondition of rigorous imprisonment for solitary confinement.

question: Under Section 5 BNS / Section 54 IPC, who has the power to commute a sentence of death to any other sentence without the consent of the offender?
options: The Appropriate Government (Central or State Government)
The Sessions Judge who passed the sentence
explanation: The Appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute a sentence of death to any other punishment provided by the Sanhita.

optionBreakdown.A: HC confirms or hears appeal, not commutation under S. 5.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Appropriate Government.
optionBreakdown.D: CJI has judicial powers, not executive commutation.

learningObjective: Identify authority for commutation of death sentence.

question: In Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978), the Supreme Court restricted the imposition of solitary confinement, holding that:
options: Solitary confinement is completely unconstitutional under Article 21
Prison authorities cannot impose solitary confinement bar without judicial court order, and it must comply with humane standards
Solitary confinement can be awarded for 1 year in terrorist cases
Convicts have no fundamental rights inside prison
explanation: The Supreme Court held that solitary confinement cannot be imposed by jail superintendents arbitrarily and must strictly conform to judicial orders under Sections 73/74.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; judicial order mandatory, humane treatment.

learningObjective: Apply constitutional limits to solitary confinement.

question: Under Section 6 BNS / Section 55 IPC, a sentence of imprisonment for life may be commuted by the Appropriate Government to imprisonment for a term not exceeding:
explanation: Section 6 BNS / Section 55 IPC provides that the Appropriate Government may commute life imprisonment to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen (14) years or fine.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; maximum 14 years.

learningObjective: Recall statutory commutation ceiling for life imprisonment.

question: What is the minimum period of actual imprisonment a life convict must undergo before premature release can be granted under CrPC S. 433A / BNSS S. 475 in capital offences?
explanation: Under Section 433A CrPC / Section 475 BNSS, where life imprisonment was imposed for an offence for which death is one of the punishments, the convict shall not be released unless they have served at least fourteen (14) years of actual imprisonment.

optionBreakdown.B: Too low.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; mandatory minimum 14 years actual custody.

learningObjective: Understand statutory minimum actual custody before remission.

question: Under Section 8(2) BNS / Section 65 IPC, the term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine shall not exceed:
options: One-half of maximum term of imprisonment for the offence
One-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence
explanation: The term of imprisonment in default of fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; one-fourth of maximum term.
optionBreakdown.C: One-third is undertrial bail threshold in S. 479.
optionBreakdown.D: Fixed limit applies only where offence is punishable with fine only.

learningObjective: Calculate default imprisonment limits for non-payment of fine.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 was EXCLUDED from the commencement notification on 1 July 2024?
explanation: Under MHA Gazette S.O. 850(E), sub-section (2) of Section 106 (hit-and-run by rash/negligent driving without reporting) was excluded from coming into force on 1 July 2024.

optionBreakdown.A: Section 106(1) is active and in force.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 106(2) hit-and-run was stayed.

learningObjective: Master the Section 106(2) BNS stay caveat.

question: What is the maximum term of imprisonment under Section 106(1) BNS (in force from 1 July 2024) for causing death by rash or negligent act (non-doctors)?
explanation: Section 106(1) BNS increases the general punishment for causing death by rash or negligent act to imprisonment extending up to five (5) years and fine (up from 2 years in IPC 304A).

optionBreakdown.A: 2 years was under old IPC Section 304A.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; up to 5 years and fine.
optionBreakdown.D: 10 years is in Section 106(2) which is not in force.

learningObjective: Identify enhanced punishment under Section 106(1) BNS.

question: Under Section 106(1) Proviso BNS, if death is caused by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, the punishment is capped at:
options: Imprisonment up to 2 years and fine
Only disciplinary reprimand by Medical Council
explanation: Section 106(1) Proviso expressly provides that if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment up to two (2) years, and fine.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; capped at 2 years and fine for doctors.
optionBreakdown.D: Criminal liability exists, but capped at 2 years.

learningObjective: Master doctor medical negligence cap in BNS.

question: What does Section 106(2) BNS (currently held in abeyance) prescribe for causing death by rash/negligent driving and escaping without reporting?
options: Imprisonment extending up to ten (10) years and fine
explanation: Section 106(2) prescribes imprisonment up to 10 years and fine for escaping without reporting to police or magistrate soon after the incident.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; up to 10 years and fine.

learningObjective: Understand stayed hit-and-run provision details.

question: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), the Supreme Court laid down that to convict a doctor for criminal medical negligence under Section 304A IPC / S. 106 BNS, the degree of negligence must be:
options: Slight carelessness or error of judgment
Gross negligence showing reckless disregard for human life
Civil negligence under the Consumer Protection Act
Any deviation from standard textbook procedures
explanation: A Three-Judge Bench held that gross negligence (Bolam test) is required for criminal liability; simple lack of care or accident does not attract criminal prosecution.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; gross negligence is mandatory for criminal conviction.
optionBreakdown.D: Professional discretion protects against minor deviations.

learningObjective: Apply Jacob Mathew criminal medical negligence doctrine.

question: What is the fundamental difference between 'Rashness' and 'Negligence' in criminal law (Cherubin Gregory v. State of Bihar)?
options: Rashness is intentional, negligence is accidental
Rashness involves running a known risk with reckless indifference; negligence involves breach of duty to take care through inadvertence
Rashness applies to driving only, negligence applies to doctors
Rashness is civil, negligence is criminal
explanation: In rashness, the actor foresees the risk but recklessly gambles with consequence; in negligence, the actor fails to exercise the care a prudent person would observe.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; conscious risk-taking vs inadvertent breach of duty.

learningObjective: Distinguish rashness from negligence.

question: A sets a live uninsulated electric wire across his garden to prevent trespassers without any warning notice. B touches the wire in the dark and dies. A is guilty of:
options: Section 106 BNS / Section 304A IPC (rash act causing death)
No offence as B was a trespasser
explanation: In Cherubin Gregory, setting a naked live wire was held to be a rash and hazardous act under Section 304A IPC / Section 106 BNS.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; rash and hazardous act causing death.
optionBreakdown.B: No specific intention to kill B.
optionBreakdown.C: Trespassers cannot be met with deadly booby traps.
optionBreakdown.D: No proper care and caution; not accident.

learningObjective: Apply rashness doctrine to hazardous acts.

question: Can Section 106 BNS / Section 304A IPC apply where death is caused with direct intention or knowledge?
options: Yes, if the victim contributed to negligence
No; Section 106 applies ONLY to cases where death is caused without intention or knowledge of causing death
Yes, in motor vehicle accidents only
explanation: Section 106 BNS / Section 304A IPC is an exclusionary provision: it applies only where the act does NOT amount to culpable homicide (i.e. neither intention nor knowledge of causing death is present).

optionBreakdown.A: Contributory negligence is no defence in crime.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; requires absence of intention and knowledge of culpable homicide.
optionBreakdown.C: Applies across all non-intentional fatal acts.

learningObjective: Understand exclusionary nature of Section 106 BNS.

question: Under Section 106(1) BNS, what type of actus reus is required?
options: Direct, proximate and efficient cause of death without intervention of another contributory cause
explanation: In Emperor v. Omkar Rampratap, Sir Lawrence Jenkins held the act must be the direct, proximate, and immediate cause of death, causa causans, not merely causa sine qua non.

optionBreakdown.B: Remote cause insufficient.

learningObjective: Apply proximate cause test in Section 106.

question: If an accident occurs on 15 August 2024 and the driver causes death by rash driving, under which provision will he be charged given the MHA Gazette S.O. 850(E)?
explanation: Because Section 106(2) is stayed and not in force, and the offence occurred after 1 July 2024, the driver must be charged under Section 106(1) BNS (up to 5 years).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 106(1) is the operational law.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 106(2) is stayed and not in force.
optionBreakdown.C: IPC was repealed for post-1 July 2024 acts.

learningObjective: Determine applicable hit-and-run charge post-July 2024.

question: The legal maxim 'Ignorantia facti excusat, ignorantia juris non excusat' means:
options: Ignorance of fact is no excuse, ignorance of law excuses
Ignorance of fact excuses, ignorance of law does not excuse
Both ignorance of fact and law excuse completely
Neither ignorance of fact nor law can ever excuse in crime
explanation: Mistake of fact is a recognized defence under Sections 14 and 17 BNS / Sections 76 and 79 IPC, but mistake of law is never an excuse.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; ignorance of fact excuses, law does not.

learningObjective: Translate foundational mistake maxim.

question: What is the key difference between Section 14 BNS (Section 76 IPC) and Section 17 BNS (Section 79 IPC)?
options: Section 14 relates to private citizens, Section 17 to judges
Section 14 deals with belief of being BOUND by law; Section 17 deals with belief of being JUSTIFIED by law
Section 14 excuses mistake of law; Section 17 excuses mistake of fact
Section 14 applies to civil wrongs; Section 17 applies to crimes
explanation: Section 14 / S. 76 covers acts done by a person bound by law or believing in good faith to be bound by law; Section 17 / S. 79 covers acts justified by law or believed in good faith to be justified by law.

optionBreakdown.A: Both apply across citizens and officials.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; bound by law vs justified by law.

learningObjective: Distinguish bound by law from justified by law.

question: A, a soldier, fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the commands of the law. A has committed:
options: No offence under Section 14 BNS / Section 76 IPC
explanation: Under Section 14 BNS / Section 76 IPC (Illustration a), a soldier obeying lawful orders of a superior in conformity with law commits no offence.

optionBreakdown.B: Exception applies.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; protected by Section 14 BNS / S. 76 IPC.

learningObjective: Apply soldier obeying lawful command exception.

question: A sees Z commit what appears to A to be a murder. A, in the exercise, to the best of his judgment exerted in good faith, of the power which the law gives to all persons of apprehending murderers in the act, seizes Z in order to bring him before the proper authorities. A has committed:
options: No offence under Section 17 BNS / Section 79 IPC
explanation: Under Section 17 BNS / Section 79 IPC (Illustration), A acts in good faith believing himself justified by law, even if Z was acting in self-defence.

optionBreakdown.B: Protected by Section 17.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; protected by belief of justification in law.

learningObjective: Apply justified by law mistake of fact illustration.

question: In R v. Tolson (1889), the defence of mistake of fact succeeded in bigamy because:
options: The second marriage was conducted in a church
Mrs. Tolson had formed a bona fide belief on reasonable grounds after 7 years of inquiry that her first husband was dead
The statute explicitly excluded mens rea
Bigamy is a civil wrong in England
explanation: The Court for Crown Cases Reserved held that an honest and reasonable belief in the existence of circumstances which, if true, would make the act innocent, is a good defence in crime.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; bona fide belief on reasonable grounds of husband's death.

learningObjective: Apply R v. Tolson mistake of fact precedent.

question: An officer of a Court, being ordered by warrant from that Court to arrest Y, and after due enquiry believing Z to be Y, arrests Z. What offence has the officer committed?
options: No offence under Section 14 BNS / Section 76 IPC
explanation: Under Illustration (b) to Section 76 IPC / Section 14 BNS, the officer, by reason of a mistake of fact and in good faith believing himself bound by law to arrest Z, commits no offence.

optionBreakdown.B: Protected by Section 14.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; mistake of fact under official warrant.

learningObjective: Apply mistake of fact to arrest warrant execution.

question: Can a foreigner arriving in India claim as a defence under Section 17 BNS / Section 79 IPC that they were ignorant of an Indian statutory regulation?
options: Yes, foreigners are entitled to presumption of ignorance
No, ignorance of law cannot be pleaded by citizens or foreigners alike
Yes, if they arrived less than 24 hours ago
Yes, with permission of the embassy
explanation: In State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, the Supreme Court confirmed that ignorance of law provides no defence to any person within Indian territory.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; ignorance of law is no defence.

learningObjective: Confirm universal bar on mistake of law.

question: Under both Sections 14 and 17 BNS, the mistake of fact MUST be accompanied by:
options: Legal advice from a senior advocate
'Good faith' (due care and attention under S. 2(11))
Prior approval of a Judicial Magistrate
explanation: Sections 14 and 17 explicitly require that the person 'in good faith believes' themselves bound or justified by law. Good faith requires due care and attention.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; good faith is mandatory.

learningObjective: Identify good faith as mandatory component.

question: A shoots at what he believes in good faith to be a tiger in thick jungle, but it turns out to be a human trespasser B. If A acted with due care and caution, A is protected under:
explanation: In State of Orissa v. Ram Bahadur Thapa (1960), shooting under a bona fide mistake of fact believing the target to be a ghost or wild animal was held protected under Section 79 IPC / Section 17 BNS.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; justified by law under mistake of fact.

learningObjective: Apply mistake of fact in hunting and wildlife scenarios.

question: If an act is prohibited by an illegal order of a military commander, can a subordinate soldier plead Section 14 BNS / Section 76 IPC if the order was manifestly illegal on its face?
options: Yes, a soldier must obey all orders blindly
No; obedience to an order which is manifestly unlawful and contrary to law affords no protection
Yes, if the commander confirms it in writing
Yes, in times of war only
explanation: The order must be in 'conformity with the commands of the law'. A soldier who shoots innocent civilians under an obviously illegal order cannot claim Section 76 / 14.

optionBreakdown.A: Blind obedience rejected in Nuremberg principles.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; manifestly illegal orders afford no defence.
optionBreakdown.D: War does not permit war crimes.

learningObjective: Analyze limits of superior orders in criminal law.

question: Under Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC, an act done by a Judge is exempt from criminal liability when acting:
options: Judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law
After receiving sanction from the Chief Justice
explanation: Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC protects acts of a Judge when acting judicially in exercise of power given, or in good faith believed to be given, by law.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; acting judicially in good faith.
optionBreakdown.D: No CJ sanction requirement in S. 77.

learningObjective: Master judicial acts criminal immunity.

question: Under Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC, a hangman who executes a sentence of death passed by a Court commits no offence, even if:
options: The Court which passed the judgment had no jurisdiction to pass it, provided the hangman in good faith believed the Court had jurisdiction
The hangman acted with personal hatred
explanation: Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC explicitly protects ministerial officers executing court warrants even if the court had no jurisdiction, provided the officer in good faith believed jurisdiction existed.

optionBreakdown.A: Innocence of prisoner doesn't affect executioner.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; protected even if court lacked jurisdiction.
optionBreakdown.C: Defective warrant without seal is invalid.
optionBreakdown.D: Must act pursuant to order in good faith.

learningObjective: Master execution of court orders exception.

question: What is the primary rationale behind Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC judicial immunity?
options: To place judges above the law
To ensure judicial independence so judges may administer justice fearlessly without apprehension of vexatious prosecutions
To grant immunity to government servants generally
To comply with international diplomatic treaties
explanation: Judicial independence under Article 50 demands that judges be insulated from criminal harassment for decisions rendered in good faith.

optionBreakdown.A: Judges are not above the law in personal crime.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; fearless and independent administration of justice.

learningObjective: Understand judicial independence in penal immunity.

question: A Magistrate sentences an accused to 6 months imprisonment under a statute which had been repealed 2 days earlier, of which the Magistrate was unaware despite exercising reasonable diligence. Is the Magistrate criminally liable for wrongful confinement?
options: Yes, ignorance of law is no excuse
No; protected under Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC as he acted judicially in good faith believing jurisdiction existed
Yes, liable for compensation under civil law only
explanation: Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC protects a Judge who in good faith believes the power to be given to him by law.

optionBreakdown.A: Judicial immunity extends to bona fide belief of law.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; protected under Section 15 BNS / S. 77 IPC.
optionBreakdown.C: Judicial Officers Protection Act 1850 bars civil liability too.

learningObjective: Apply judicial immunity to belief of statutory authority.

question: Does Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC protect a police officer who executes a search warrant which has expired on its face?
options: No; Section 16 protects acts done pursuant to a judgment or order whilst such order remains in force
Yes, if the officer was busy
Yes, if the magistrate later ratifies it
explanation: Section 16 protects acts done while the order remains in force. Executing an expired or cancelled warrant is unlawful.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; order must be in force.
optionBreakdown.D: Ex-post ratification cannot legalize illegal search.

learningObjective: Identify limits of ministerial execution protection.

question: A Judge who accepts a bribe to acquit an accused in a criminal case can claim:
options: Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC immunity because he was presiding in court
No protection under Section 15 / 77 because bribery is not an act done in good faith or judicially
explanation: Accepting a bribe is a corrupt criminal act, not an act done judicially in good faith; judicial immunity is completely unavailable (K. Veeraswami v. Union of India).

optionBreakdown.A: Immunity covers judicial acts, not corrupt crimes.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; bribery destroys good faith and judicial character.
optionBreakdown.C: Impeachment is for removal; criminal trial proceeds after CJI sanction.

provision: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India, (1991) 3 SCC 655
learningObjective: Demarcate corrupt acts from protected judicial acts.

question: Under Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC, the officer executing the order of the court must show that:
options: He read the entire trial judgment
He acted in good faith believing that the Court had jurisdiction to pass the order
The order was confirmed by the Supreme Court
The accused consented to the execution
explanation: The statutory condition in Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC is that the person executing the order in good faith believes that the Court had such jurisdiction.

optionBreakdown.A: Executioner need not read full judgment.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; good faith belief in court jurisdiction.

learningObjective: Recall statutory condition for warrant execution.

question: A bailiff enters B's house with a valid civil warrant of attachment issued by a competent court. B resists and uses force. Is the bailiff guilty of criminal trespass?
options: No, protected under Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC
Yes, civil court orders do not protect against criminal trespass
Yes, if property belonged to third party
explanation: The bailiff is executing an order of a court of justice in force and is fully protected under Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC.

optionBreakdown.A: Protest does not invalidate legal process.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; protected by Section 16 BNS / Section 78 IPC.
optionBreakdown.C: Orders of civil courts are fully covered.
optionBreakdown.D: Bona fide execution under warrant is protected.

learningObjective: Apply court order protection to civil execution bailiffs.

question: Which statute works alongside Section 15 BNS / Section 77 IPC to provide comprehensive protection to judicial officers?
options: Judicial Officers Protection Act, 1850 & Judges (Protection) Act, 1985
explanation: The Judicial Officers Protection Act, 1850 (civil immunity) and Judges (Protection) Act, 1985 (bar on criminal/civil proceedings) complement Section 77 IPC / Section 15 BNS.

optionBreakdown.B: Advocates Act regulates bar.

learningObjective: Identify statutory framework protecting judicial officers.

question: If a court issues a warrant directing arrest of A, but the constable intentionally arrests B because of personal rivalry, can the constable plead Section 16 BNS?
options: No; the constable did not act in good faith pursuant to the warrant
Yes, constable can rectify the mistake later
Yes, with permission of the SP
explanation: Intentional arrest of a different person out of personal rivalry completely lacks good faith and violates the warrant; Section 16 affords zero protection.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; lack of good faith and intentional malice excludes protection.
optionBreakdown.C: Subsequent release does not wipe criminal liability.

learningObjective: Distinguish intentional malice from protected execution.

question: Under Section 18 BNS / Section 80 IPC (Accident), which of the following is NOT an essential ingredient?
options: Done without any criminal intention or knowledge
Done in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means
Done after obtaining prior permission of police authorities
explanation: Police permission is not an element of Section 18 BNS / Section 80 IPC. The ingredients are: accident, no criminal intention/knowledge, lawful act, lawful manner/means, with proper care and caution.

optionBreakdown.B: Essential ingredient.
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; police permission is not an ingredient.

learningObjective: Identify statutory ingredients of Accident defence.

question: A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a man who is standing by. If there was no want of proper caution on the part of A, A's act is:
options: Excusable as an accident under Section 18 BNS / Section 80 IPC
Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
explanation: Under Section 18 BNS / Section 80 IPC (Illustration), A's act is excusable and not an offence because it was a lawful act done in a lawful manner with proper care and caution.

optionBreakdown.B: No criminal intention or knowledge.
optionBreakdown.C: No want of caution, so negligence excluded.

learningObjective: Apply classic hatchet accident illustration.

question: The maxim 'Quod necessitas non habet legem' forms the philosophical foundation of:
explanation: The maxim means 'Necessity knows no law' and underpins the defence of Necessity in Section 19 BNS / Section 81 IPC.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Necessity knows no law.

learningObjective: Match legal maxim with Necessity defence.

question: In the landmark English authority R v. Dudley and Stephens (1884), the defence of necessity was rejected because:
options: Self-preservation does not justify the deliberate killing of an innocent person to save one's own life
The ship was registered in Australia
explanation: Lord Coleridge C.J. held that necessity can never justify taking the life of an innocent person to preserve one's own life.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; self-preservation cannot justify murder.
optionBreakdown.D: Consent to death is no defence under law.

learningObjective: Apply R v. Dudley and Stephens necessity doctrine.

question: A, the captain of a vessel, suddenly finds himself in such a position that before he can stop, he must inevitably run down a boat B with 30 passengers, unless he alters course, in which case he must run down boat C with 2 passengers. A alters course and runs down boat C in good faith to save 30 passengers. A is protected under:
explanation: Under Section 19 BNS / Section 81 IPC (Illustration), A is not guilty of an offence if he acted without criminal intention and in good faith to avoid greater harm to the 30 passengers.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; prevention of greater harm under necessity.
optionBreakdown.D: Loss of life is not trivial.

learningObjective: Apply vessel collision necessity illustration.

question: The doctrine of 'Doli Incapax' (incapable of committing crime) is codified under Section 20 BNS / Section 82 IPC for a child under the age of:
explanation: Section 20 BNS / Section 82 IPC enacts an absolute irrebuttable presumption: 'Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.'

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; strictly under seven years of age.
optionBreakdown.D: Juvenile Justice Act covers minors under 18.

learningObjective: Recall the age limit for absolute Doli Incapax.

question: Under Section 21 BNS / Section 83 IPC, a child above seven years and under twelve years of age is immune from criminal liability ONLY IF the child:
options: Has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion
Did not use a deadly weapon
Acted under direction of his parents
explanation: Section 21 BNS / Section 83 IPC establishes a rebuttable presumption of doli incapax; liability depends on whether the child has attained sufficient maturity of understanding.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; immature understanding is the statutory test.
optionBreakdown.C: Weapon used may be evidence of maturity.
optionBreakdown.D: Parental command is not the test.

learningObjective: Master rebuttable infancy presumption.

question: A 10-year-old child picks up a gold necklace from a shop, immediately conceals it in his shoe, and sells it to a jeweller for cash. Is the child protected under Section 21 BNS / Section 83 IPC?
options: Yes, every child under 12 has absolute immunity
No; hiding the necklace in the shoe and selling it demonstrates sufficient maturity of understanding
Yes, provided the parents return the money
Yes, child can never be prosecuted under any law
explanation: In Ulla Mahapatra (1950), conduct such as concealing the stolen property or weapon was held to demonstrate mature understanding, defeating the Section 83 / 21 defence.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; conduct exhibits maturity of understanding.
optionBreakdown.D: Subject to Juvenile Justice Act procedure.

learningObjective: Apply maturity of understanding test in children.

question: What type of presumption is enacted under Section 20 BNS / Section 82 IPC regarding a 6-year-old child?
options: Conclusive and irrebuttable presumption of law
Presumption of fact under Section 114 Evidence Act
explanation: The presumption that a child under 7 years cannot commit a crime is conclusive and irrebuttable; no evidence can be led by prosecution to show the child knew the act was wrong.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; conclusive, irrebuttable presumption of law.

learningObjective: Classify infancy presumption type.

question: In Bishambhar v. Roomal (1951), villagers blackened the face of a molester and paraded him on a donkey to prevent caste rioting. The defence of necessity under Section 81 IPC failed because:
options: Harm caused was intentionally inflicted directly upon an individual, which cannot be justified under Section 81
Section 81 applies only to fires and shipwrecks
explanation: Section 81 protects acts done without criminal intent to avoid greater harm, but does not legalize the intentional commission of an offence against an individual as private vigilante punishment.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; intentional private punishment not covered by necessity.
optionBreakdown.C: Section 81 is general, not restricted to ships.
optionBreakdown.D: Police notice not the core holding.

learningObjective: Understand limits of necessity against private vengeance.

question: Section 22 BNS / Section 84 IPC is founded upon which celebrated English common law rules?
options: The American Model Penal Code Rule
explanation: Section 22 BNS / Section 84 IPC codifies the classic M'Naghten Rules formulated by the House of Lords in 1843.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; M'Naghten Rules (1843).
optionBreakdown.C: Irresistible impulse is not recognized under S. 84.

learningObjective: Identify common law source of Indian insanity defence.

question: What is the crucial statutory standard for legal insanity under Section 22 BNS / Section 84 IPC?
options: Mental depression and psychological mood swings
Incapable of knowing the nature of the act, OR that it is either wrong or contrary to law, by reason of unsoundness of mind
Subnormal IQ certified by a psychologist
Irresistible impulse driving the accused to commit murder
explanation: The cognitive impairment must be such that the person is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it is wrong or contrary to law.

optionBreakdown.A: Medical depression is not legal insanity.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; statutory cognitive incapacity test.
optionBreakdown.C: Low IQ is not legal insanity.
optionBreakdown.D: Irresistible impulse does not excuse in India.

learningObjective: Recall statutory test for legal insanity.

question: What is the fundamental distinction between 'Medical Insanity' and 'Legal Insanity' (Surendra Mishra v. State of Jharkhand)?
options: Medical insanity is temporary, legal insanity is permanent
Every person who is mentally ill (medical insanity) is not legally insane; legal insanity requires total cognitive incapacity at the time of committing the act
Medical insanity excuses crime, legal insanity does not
Legal insanity is determined by doctors, medical insanity by judges
explanation: Medical insanity covers all psychological disorders, but legal insanity under Section 84 requires cognitive incapacity to know right from wrong at the exact time of the offence.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; legal insanity requires cognitive destruction at time of act.
optionBreakdown.D: Judges determine legal insanity based on law.

learningObjective: Distinguish legal insanity from medical insanity.

question: Under Section 105 Evidence Act / Section 108 BSA, upon whom does the burden of proving legal insanity rest?
options: Upon the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt
Upon the accused, by a preponderance of probabilities
Upon the medical board appointed by court
explanation: The court presumes the absence of circumstances bringing the case within general exceptions. The burden of proving insanity is on the accused, dischargeable on a preponderance of probabilities (Dahyabhai).

optionBreakdown.A: Prosecution proves guilt, not general exceptions.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; burden on accused on preponderance of probability.

provision: Dahyabhai v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1964 SC 1563
learningObjective: Master burden of proof in insanity defence.

question: Under Section 23 BNS / Section 85 IPC, involuntary intoxication is a complete defence ONLY IF the thing which intoxicated the person was administered:
options: Without his knowledge or against his will
In an alcoholic beverage at a social party
explanation: Section 23 BNS / Section 85 IPC explicitly requires that the intoxicating substance was administered to the person 'without his knowledge or against his will'.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; without knowledge or against will.
optionBreakdown.C: Voluntary drinking at parties is not involuntary.
optionBreakdown.D: Sleeping administration is only one example of lack of knowledge.

learningObjective: Identify core element of involuntary intoxication.

question: In Basdev v. State of Pepsu (1956), concerning voluntary intoxication under Section 86 IPC / Section 24 BNS, the Supreme Court held that:
options: While knowledge is attributed to the drunken accused as if he were sober, intention cannot be automatically presumed and must be gathered from surrounding facts
A drunken person is presumed to have intended every consequence
explanation: Under Section 86, the law presumes knowledge on par with a sober man, but intention must be inferred from surrounding circumstances and cannot be blindly imputed.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; knowledge is presumed, intention is gathered from facts.

learningObjective: Master Basdev doctrine on voluntary intoxication.

question: A gets voluntarily intoxicated at a wedding. When requested to step aside by a boy B, A draws a pistol, says 'I will shoot you if you don't move', and shoots B dead. A's defence of voluntary intoxication will:
options: Fail, because drawing a pistol and uttering threats demonstrates clear intention and knowledge under Basdev principles
Reduce the offence to simple hurt
explanation: The facts are directly identical to Basdev v. State of Pepsu; drawing a weapon and uttering threats showed that A's mind was capable of forming the intention to shoot.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; intention and knowledge demonstrated.
optionBreakdown.C: Fatal gunshot is not simple hurt.

provision: Basdev v. State of Pepsu, AIR 1956 SC 488
learningObjective: Apply voluntary intoxication principles to shooting incident.

question: Does the defence of 'Irresistible Impulse' excuse a crime under Section 22 BNS / Section 84 IPC?
options: Yes, mental impulse is recognized in Section 84
No; Section 84 requires cognitive incapacity; emotional or uncontrollable impulse where the accused knows the act is wrong affords no legal defence
Yes, if certified by a psychiatrist
explanation: Indian law strictly adheres to the cognitive test of M'Naghten; irresistible impulse where the actor knows the act is wrong does not satisfy Section 84.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; irresistible impulse does not excuse under Indian law.
optionBreakdown.C: Crimes of passion may at best attract Exception 1 to S. 101/300.

provision: State of M.P. v. Ahmadulla, AIR 1961 SC 998
learningObjective: Confirm rejection of irresistible impulse in Indian law.

question: Delirium Tremens (temporary insanity caused by habitual long-term drinking) is treated under criminal law as:
options: Unsoundness of mind (insanity) under Section 84 / Section 22 BNS
explanation: Under settled law, madness or delirium tremens produced by drunkenness is treated as ordinary insanity under Section 84 / 22, not as voluntary intoxication.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; treated as insanity under Section 84 / 22 BNS.

learningObjective: Classify Delirium Tremens in criminal defence.

question: At what precise moment must the unsoundness of mind exist for Section 22 BNS / Section 84 IPC to apply?
options: At the time of committing the act
At the time of arrest by police
explanation: The statutory phrase is: 'who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing...'. Antecedent or subsequent insanity is only relevant to infer state of mind at the time of the act.

optionBreakdown.A: Unsoundness at trial leads to inquiry under BNSS 367.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; at the exact time of doing the act.
optionBreakdown.D: Prior history is evidential, not conclusive.

learningObjective: Pinpoint the crucial timing for insanity defence.

question: The common law maxim 'Volenti non fit injuria' means:
options: An act done under necessity is lawful
No injury is done to one who consents
Ignorance of law does not excuse
The King can do no wrong
explanation: Volenti non fit injuria underpins the consent exceptions in Sections 25 to 29 BNS / Sections 87 to 91 IPC.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; harm suffered with consent is not legal injury.

learningObjective: Translate Volenti non fit injuria.

question: Under Section 28 BNS / Section 90 IPC, consent is NOT valid if given:
options: By a person above 18 years of age
Under fear of injury, or misconception of fact, or by a person of unsound mind, intoxicated, or under twelve years of age
explanation: Section 28 BNS / Section 90 IPC defines vitiated consent: fear of injury, misconception of fact, child under 12 years, or person of unsound mind / intoxicated.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; fear, misconception, child <12, intoxication/insanity.

learningObjective: Identify grounds vitiating consent in penal law.

question: Under Section 25 BNS / Section 87 IPC (harm consented in sports), consent cannot justify an act which is intended or known to be likely to cause:
explanation: Section 25 BNS / Section 87 IPC applies only to acts not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt (e.g. fencing, cricket).

optionBreakdown.A: Simple hurt is covered by sport consent.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; cannot consent to death or grievous hurt under S. 87.

learningObjective: Recall limits of consent in games and sports.

question: Under Section 32 BNS / Section 94 IPC (Duress / Compulsion), which two offences are STRICTLY EXCLUDED and can NEVER be excused by threats of instant death?
options: Murder and offences against the State punishable with death
explanation: Section 32 BNS / Section 94 IPC explicitly excludes Murder and offences against the State punishable with death (e.g. waging war).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; murder and capital state offences are never excused by duress.
optionBreakdown.B: Property crimes can be excused by duress.
optionBreakdown.C: Extortion/kidnapping can be excused if compelled.

learningObjective: Identify offences excluded from duress defence.

question: A is seized by a gang of dacoits and threatened with instant death if he does not force open the door of a house with his blacksmith tools. A opens the door. What offence has A committed?
options: No offence under Section 32 BNS / Section 94 IPC
explanation: Under Illustration (a) to Section 94 IPC / Section 32 BNS, a blacksmith forced by threats of instant death commits no offence as he did not place himself in that position voluntarily.

optionBreakdown.B: Protected by duress.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; protected by Section 32 BNS / S. 94 IPC.

learningObjective: Apply blacksmith duress illustration.

question: Under Section 33 BNS / Section 95 IPC, the maxim 'De minimis non curat lex' means:
options: The law does not concern itself with trifles
explanation: De minimis non curat lex means the law does not take account of trifles; harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain is excused.

optionBreakdown.B: Ignorantia facti.

learningObjective: Translate De minimis non curat lex.

question: A accidentally brushes his elbow against B while boarding a crowded Mumbai local train, causing minor contact. B files a complaint of criminal force against A. The court will dismiss the complaint under:
options: Section 33 BNS / Section 95 IPC (Act causing slight harm / De minimis)
explanation: Brushing past in crowded public transit is a classic trifle of daily life protected under Section 95 IPC / Section 33 BNS.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; trivial harm under Section 33 BNS / Section 95 IPC.

learningObjective: Apply trivial acts exception to crowded transit contact.

question: Under Section 27 BNS / Section 89 IPC, who can give consent for an act done in good faith for the benefit of a child under twelve years of age or person of unsound mind?
options: The guardian or other person having lawful charge of such person
explanation: Section 27 BNS / Section 89 IPC allows consent to be given by or on behalf of the child or person of unsound mind by their guardian or lawful custodian.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; guardian or person having lawful charge.

learningObjective: Identify who consents for minors under 12.

question: A, a surgeon, seeing a child suffer an accident which is likely to prove fatal unless an operation be immediately performed, performs the operation without waiting to recover the guardian's consent. The child dies during operation. A is protected under:
explanation: Under Section 29 BNS / Section 92 IPC (Illustration c), performing an emergency surgical operation in good faith for a patient's benefit without consent when consent cannot be obtained in time is protected.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; emergency act without consent under Section 29 BNS / S. 92 IPC.
optionBreakdown.C: Operation is intentional act, not accident.

learningObjective: Apply emergency medical intervention without consent.

question: If a person voluntarily joins a gang of dacoits knowing their character, can he afterwards plead duress under Section 32 BNS / Section 94 IPC when compelled by the gang to commit robbery?
options: Yes, threats of death always excuse
No; Explanation 1 to Section 32 BNS / Section 94 IPC explicitly bars a person who voluntarily placed himself in such situation from pleading duress
Yes, if he was a minor
explanation: Explanation 1 to Section 94 IPC / Section 32 BNS provides that a person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, cannot take the benefit of this exception.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; voluntary gang membership excludes duress defence.

learningObjective: Analyze self-induced duress exclusion.

question: The right of private defence under Sections 34 to 44 BNS / Sections 96 to 106 IPC is:
options: A punitive right to punish criminals
A preventive and protective right to defend oneself and others from unlawful aggression
An offensive right to eliminate enemies
explanation: Private defence is strictly defensive and preventive; it is not a right of retribution, punishment, or revenge.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; preventive and protective right.

learningObjective: Define the legal character of private defence.

question: Under Section 37 BNS / Section 99 IPC, there is NO right of private defence against an act done by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, UNLESS the act causes reasonable apprehension of:
explanation: Section 37 BNS / Section 99 IPC provides that there is no right of private defence against a public servant unless the act causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

optionBreakdown.A: Wrongful arrest does not justify violent defence.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; death or grievous hurt apprehension restores defence.
optionBreakdown.C: Reputation not grounds for violent resistance.
optionBreakdown.D: Financial loss does not justify physical resistance.

learningObjective: Identify when private defence lies against public servants.

question: Under Section 37(3) BNS / Section 99(3) IPC, there is NO right of private defence in cases in which there is:
options: Time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities
A large crowd witnessing the event
explanation: Where there is reasonable opportunity and time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities (police/magistrate), the right of private defence does not arise.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; recourse to public authorities bars private defence.

learningObjective: Recall the recourse to public authorities limitation.

question: How much harm may be inflicted in the exercise of the right of private defence under Section 37(4) BNS / Section 99(4) IPC?
options: Any amount of harm including death in all cases
No more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence (Proportionality)
explanation: Section 37(4) BNS / Section 99(4) IPC enacts the rule of proportionality: the right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for defence.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; proportionality test: no more harm than necessary.

learningObjective: Master proportionality rule in private defence.

question: Under Section 38 BNS / Section 100 IPC, which of the following assaults justifies causing the DEATH of the assailant in private defence of body?
options: Assault with a small stick on the arm
An assault with the intention of committing rape
explanation: Section 38 BNS / Section 100 IPC specifies grounds where death may be caused, including assault with intention of committing rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping/abduction, or acid attack.

optionBreakdown.A: Stick bruise does not justify death.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; assault with intention of committing rape justifies causing death.
optionBreakdown.C: Simple hurt does not justify death.

learningObjective: Identify grounds where causing death is justified in body defence.

question: Which ground for causing death in private defence of the body was added to Section 100 IPC in 2013 and preserved in Section 38 BNS?
options: An act of throwing or administering acid, or an attempt to do so
explanation: Clause 'Seventhly' was added by Criminal Law Amendment Act 2013: an act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw acid causing apprehension of grievous hurt justifies causing death.

optionBreakdown.B: Correct; acid attack clause justifies causing death.

learningObjective: Recall 2013 acid attack amendment in Section 100/38.

question: Under Section 41 BNS / Section 103 IPC, in which property offence does the right of private defence of property extend to causing the DEATH of the wrongdoer?
options: Theft of cash from a shop during daytime
explanation: Under Section 41 BNS / Section 103 IPC, private defence of property extends to causing death in: Robbery, House-breaking by night, Mischief by fire to human dwelling/tent/vessel, or Theft/Mischief/House-trespass causing apprehension of death/grievous hurt.

optionBreakdown.A: Simple daytime theft does not justify death.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Robbery is an express statutory ground.

learningObjective: Identify property offences where causing death is justified.

question: When does the right of private defence of the body COMMENCE and how long does it CONTINUE under Section 39 BNS / Section 102 IPC?
options: Commences when actual blow is struck; continues until police arrive
Commences as soon as reasonable apprehension of danger to body arises from attempt or threat; continues as long as such apprehension continues
Commences only after filing an FIR; continues during trial
Commences upon verbal challenge; continues permanently
explanation: Section 39 BNS / Section 102 IPC provides that the right commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger arises from an attempt or threat, though the offence may not have been committed; and continues as long as apprehension continues.

optionBreakdown.A: Victim need not wait for first blow.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; reasonable apprehension starts and bounds the right.

learningObjective: Master duration and commencement of private defence.

question: A is attacked by a mob who attempt to murder him. He cannot effectually exercise his right of private defence without firing on the mob, and he cannot fire without risk of harming innocent young children who are mingled with the mob. If A fires and kills an innocent child, A has committed:
options: No offence under Section 44 BNS / Section 106 IPC
explanation: Section 44 BNS / Section 106 IPC explicitly provides that if in exercise of private defence against deadly assault the defender is so situated that he cannot exercise it without risk of harm to an innocent person, his right extends to running that risk.

optionBreakdown.A: Protected by Section 44 BNS / S. 106 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Protected by Section 44.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; classic innocent bystander risk illustration.

learningObjective: Apply innocent bystander risk in private defence.

question: Under Section 41 BNS / Section 103 IPC, does the right to cause death in defence of property extend to 'House-breaking by DAY'?
options: Yes, house-breaking at any time justifies causing death
No; Section 41 BNS / Section 103 IPC specifically restricts this right to 'House-breaking by NIGHT'
Yes, if the house-breaker is armed
Yes, if the house contains gold
explanation: Section 41 BNS / Section 103 IPC specifies 'Secondly — House-breaking by night'. Simple daytime house-breaking does NOT extend to causing death unless it creates apprehension of death or grievous hurt under clause Fourthly.

optionBreakdown.A: Distinction between day and night is vital.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; specifically house-breaking by night.
optionBreakdown.C: Unless weapon causes apprehension of death.

learningObjective: Distinguish daytime from nighttime house-breaking in private defence.
